chapter: Regional bands, politics and travel abroad
title: Touring the Soviet Union with Goodman in 1962
summary: Wilson describes huge enthusiastic crowds, bows after the show, and audiences clapping on two and four, which his son links to folk music.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: Uh huh. And of course, you were in the Soviet Union with Benny, too.
Yeah, with Benny Goodman, on a tour, yeah.
What year was that?
How'd you like that?

That was tremendous, too. That band was like in the old days at the Paramount Theatre. Some of those big giant halls, they would have 10,000 people in them, and sometimes they wouldn't go home. We followed Goodman, we would take bow after bow, the band would take a bow, and then we'd go change clothes and take a bow with our street clothes on. Goodman came out once or twice to take a bow with his hat and coat on, on stage, and still the people wouldn't go! Several times.
I'll be ...

So we'd just have to get on the bus and go back to the hotel. You know, it's a very policed state, but a lot of times the crowd would get enthused, and they'd rush down and run over the police, and everybody would get out and crowd around the stage, just like they used to do at the Gray Stone Ballroom in Detroit or the kids at the Paramount in New York or the Earl Theatre in Philadelphia. The
jazz music would get to them, that's all.

And interestingly enough, the Soviet Union was one phenomenon we couldn't understand, that whole band -- when the people got worked up or the music, and they wanted to show their involvement, they would clap on two and four. Like the audiences at the Apollo or the Negro ghetto audiences.
Uh huh.

Like the Regal in Chicago. But like at the Paramount, that was home for this stuff, as so much jazz was playing, and half the audience would be on one and three. So in the Soviet Union, everybody was on two and four, and we couldn't figure that out.
That's amazing.
Unless the native Russian folk music is a strong two-four; that's what Ted was saying. I discussed that with him once.
Well, he's very literate.
Yes, he studied some -- you know, he knows the music of the world.
Yes, sure does.
He said he played some -- he used to play in a balalaika group.
That's your son, Ted, now.
Yeah, uh huh-- and they want him to play strong on the bass on one and three, because all the others -- it's a very powerful two and four, ba-- ba, ba, ba -- the balalaika--
so he thinks that two-four feeling is rooted in folk music and they can hear it immediately in the jazz.
It's amazing, the international language of notes, music, of sound. You don't see a person's color, it's how he sounds, is how you respect him.
